stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 1.4 key concept: the Inca state organized labor, records, and roads to govern a large empire
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing Inca administration, c. 1438–1532
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Inca Empire, which expanded rapidly from Cuzco after about 1438 under the ruler Pachacuti, had no money economy and no written script like those of Afro-Eurasian states. Instead the state organized the labor of its subjects. Households owed the mit'a, a rotating labor service, which built roads, terraces, and storehouses and supplied soldiers. In return the state stored food and cloth for use in famine and held feasts at which rulers rewarded loyalty.

Officials recorded census data, labor obligations, and the contents of storehouses on quipus, knotted cords that trained specialists could read. The Inca also moved communities, called mitmaq colonists, to newly conquered regions to farm and to spread the Quechua language and Inca administration. A network of roads linked the four quarters of the empire.

stimulusBlocks.source: battuta-gibb-1929
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Ibn Battuta, Muslim legal scholar from Morocco who traveled c. 1325–1354, account dictated to the writer Ibn Juzayy, 1355, describing his stay in the Mali Empire, 1352–1353
stimulusBlocks.citation: Ibn Battuta, Travels in Asia and Africa, 1325–1354, trans. H. A. R. Gibb (London: George Routledge & Sons, 1929), ch. 14. Checked against Internet Archive scan travelsinasiaafr0000ibnb, scan pp. 351–352.
stimulusBlocks.note: Bracketed words replace the translator's dated term for West Africans. “White men” refers to North African and Arab visitors and merchants.
stimulusBlocks.text:
[The people of Mali] possess some admirable qualities. They are seldom unjust, and have a greater abhorrence of injustice than any other people. Their sultan shows no mercy to anyone who is guilty of the least act of it. There is complete security in their country. Neither traveller nor inhabitant in it has anything to fear from robbers or men of violence. They do not confiscate the property of any white man who dies in their country, even if it be uncounted wealth. On the contrary, they give it into the charge of some trustworthy person among the whites, until the rightful heir takes possession of it. They are careful to observe the hours of prayer, and assiduous in attending them in congregations, and in bringing up their children to them. . . .

Yet another is their zeal for learning the Koran by heart. . . . Among their bad qualities are the following. . . . Then there is their custom of putting dust and ashes on their heads, as a mark of respect, and the grotesque ceremonies we have described when the poets recite their verses.

Ibn Battuta was a visitor from Morocco, not an official of Mali.
He was not a West African and did not belong to the court.
He traveled as a scholar and not primarily as a merchant.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.1 key concept: the Qing dynasty expanded and governed China by combining Manchu and Chinese institutions
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the rise and expansion of the Qing dynasty, 1644–1760
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Qing dynasty began as a Manchu state in northeastern Asia. In 1644 Manchu armies, invited into Beijing to help put down a rebellion, took power and established Qing rule over China. The Manchu rulers organized their soldiers into banners, military units that included Manchu, Mongol, and Han Chinese families, and they kept the Confucian examination system so that educated Han scholars could serve as officials. Under the emperors Kangxi and Qianlong, Qing armies conquered Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet, and Xinjiang, roughly doubling the empire's size by the mid-1700s.

The Qing required Han men to wear the queue, a Manchu hairstyle, as a sign of submission, but they let Tibetan Buddhist and Mongol institutions govern daily life in many frontier regions.

Daimyo ruled domains in Tokugawa Japan.
questions.distinguisher: The Mughal mansabdar system also ranked officials by the ruler's appointment, but it belonged to a different empire.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 3.3 key concept: the Catholic Reformation responded to Protestant challenges through reform and missionary work
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the Catholic Reformation, 1540–1600
stimulusBlocks.text:
In response to the Protestant Reformation, the Catholic Church held the Council of Trent between 1545 and 1563. The council reaffirmed teachings that Protestants rejected, including the authority of the pope and the value of both faith and good works. It also ended the sale of indulgences, required bishops to live in their dioceses, and ordered seminaries to train priests.

The Society of Jesus, founded by Ignatius of Loyola and approved in 1540, ran schools across Europe and sent missionaries to Asia and the Americas, such as Francis Xavier in India and Japan. Catholic rulers, including Philip II of Spain, also used the Inquisition to suppress heresy.

By the 1700s, Spanish America had a social hierarchy based on birth and ancestry. At the top were peninsulares, officials born in Spain, who held the highest offices in government and the Church. options.prompt: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 2.6 key concept: pandemic disease spread along trade networks and changed labor and society
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing historians' views of the Black Death, 1346–1400
stimulusBlocks.text:
The Black Death, a pandemic of plague that reached the Mediterranean in 1347, killed an estimated third to half of Europe's people within a few years. Historians have long linked the plague to Mongol-era trade networks: plague bacteria circulated among rodents in Central Asia, and traders, armies, and ships carried infected fleas along the routes that joined Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.

Many historians argue that the plague's long-term effects included higher wages for surviving workers in Western Europe, because labor had become scarce. Landlords tried to hold wages down, and peasants in several regions resisted, but the old system of serfdom weakened. Other historians stress that effects varied by region and that some landlords, especially in Eastern Europe, tightened their control over peasants instead.

parts.prompt: Identify ONE long-term effect of the plague that the passage attributes to labor scarcity in Western Europe.
criteria: States a specific effect named in the passage.
Connects the effect to the shortage of workers.

model.answer: Labor scarcity raised the wages of surviving workers in Western Europe.
model.prove: The passage says that because labor had become scarce, surviving workers could earn higher wages.
model.explain: With fewer workers available, landlords and employers had to compete for them, which strengthened workers' bargaining power.

parts.alternatives: The weakening of serfdom in Western Europe also earns the point.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE piece of historical evidence, not mentioned in the passage, that supports the argument that labor scarcity changed the relationship between landlords and peasants in Western Europe.
criteria: Gives a specific example beyond the passage.
Explains how it shows landlords and peasants responding to labor scarcity.

model.answer: English landlords and officials tried to hold wages down, and peasants resisted.
model.prove: Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers in 1351 to cap wages at pre-plague levels, and English peasants joined the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.
model.explain: The need for a law to fix wages shows that workers were demanding more, and the revolt shows that peasants were willing to challenge landlords and the crown over their obligations.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain that many English peasants converted their labor obligations to money rents or left manors for better terms elsewhere.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way the spread of the plague in the 1300s shows connections among regions of Afro-Eurasia.
criteria: Names a specific route, place, or group.
Explains how the connection carried the plague.

model.answer: The plague spread along trade routes that linked Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
model.prove: In 1346 plague reached the Black Sea port of Caffa, and Genoese merchant ships carried it to Sicily and other Mediterranean ports in 1347.
model.explain: Ships and caravans moved infected rats and fleas along with goods, so the commercial networks that brought wealth also carried disease.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain how Mongol-controlled overland routes through Central Asia carried plague westward, or how plague spread along the Silk Roads and Indian Ocean ports.

Today, on the continent of Africa, nearly 30 million people have the AIDS virus - including three million children under the age of 15. There are whole countries in Africa where more than one-third of the adult population carries the infection. More than four million require immediate drug treatment. Yet across that continent, only 50,000 AIDS victims - only 50,000 - are receiving the medicine they need. . . .

AIDS can be prevented. Anti-retroviral drugs can extend life for many years. And the cost of those drugs has dropped from 12,000 dollars a year to under 300 dollars a year - which places a tremendous possibility within our grasp. . . .

I ask the Congress to commit 15 billion dollars over the next five years, including nearly ten billion dollars in new money, to turn the tide against AIDS in the most afflicted nations of Africa and the Caribbean.

model.answer: Bush says the cost of anti-retroviral drugs had fallen sharply.

model.explain: Lower prices made it realistic for governments to treat millions of people, so a large aid program could save many lives.

model.answer: Faster and cheaper travel allowed diseases to move across regions quickly.
model.prove: Jet air travel after the 1950s carried millions of passengers across continents, and migration from rural areas to crowded cities increased contact among people.

model.explain: Cooperation among governments allowed vaccination teams to reach remote areas, showing that organized international action could defeat a disease that had killed millions.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain the development of antibiotics such as penicillin, the polio vaccines of the 1950s, or antiretroviral treatment for HIV.

model.answer: Akbar ended the jizya, the tax paid by non-Muslims.
model.prove: He abolished the jizya in 1564, and he also appointed Hindu Rajput leaders to high ranks in the imperial service.
model.explain: Removing the tax and opening high offices gave Hindu elites a stake in Mughal rule and helped Akbar govern a population that was mostly Hindu.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also identify his policy of sulh-i-kul, or “peace with all,” his marriages to Rajput princesses, or his sponsorship of discussions among scholars of different faiths.

criteria: Names a specific policy of Aurangzeb.
Describes how it differed from Akbar's approach.

model.answer: Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya on non-Muslims.
model.prove: In 1679 he restored the tax that Akbar had abolished, and he ordered some Hindu temples destroyed.
model.explain: These measures emphasized the privileged position of Islam and ended Akbar's effort to treat Hindus as full partners in the state.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also describe Aurangzeb's execution of the Sikh guru Tegh Bahadur in 1675 or his stricter enforcement of Islamic law.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way religious policy affected the stability of the Mughal Empire in the late 1600s and early 1700s.
criteria: Names a specific group, region, or event.
Explains how religious policy contributed to instability.

model.answer: Stricter policies contributed to revolts that weakened the empire.
model.prove: The Marathas under Shivaji and his successors resisted Mughal rule in the Deccan, and Sikhs under Guru Gobind Singh organized as a military community after the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur.
model.explain: Aurangzeb's long wars against these groups drained the treasury and army, and after his death in 1707 the Mughal state lost control of many provinces.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain Rajput resentment of Aurangzeb's policies or the empire's loss of Hindu allies who had been central to Akbar's system.

The cause of America is in a great measure the cause of all mankind. . . .

Society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil; in its worst state an intolerable one . . . .

documents.attribution: John Stuart Mill, British philosopher and official of the East India Company from 1823 to 1858, On Liberty, 1859
documents.content: It is, perhaps, hardly necessary to say that this doctrine is meant to apply only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties. . . . For the same reason, we may leave out of consideration those backward states of society in which the race itself may be considered as in its nonage. . . . Despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement, and the means justified by actually effecting that end. Liberty, as a principle, has no application to any state of things anterior to the time when mankind have become capable of being improved by free and equal discussion. Until then, there is nothing for them but implicit obedience to an Akbar or a Charlemagne, if they are so fortunate as to find one.

options.modelResponse:
In 1750, most societies were organized around hierarchies of birth: monarchs and nobles ruled, women had few legal rights, and European empires governed colonies overseas. The Enlightenment questioned those arrangements by arguing that people had natural rights and that reason, not tradition, should guide government. Soon afterward, the Industrial Revolution created factories, a wage-earning working class, and a new middle class that sought influence.

Between 1750 and 1900, new ideas about government, labor, and economic life challenged hierarchies based on birth and monarchy, but they also created or justified new hierarchies of class, gender, and empire, so the challenge was significant but uneven.

Several documents show direct challenges to traditional authority. Thomas Paine argued that "society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil" and mocked the idea that a continent should be governed by an island (Document 1). Writing as a pamphleteer in Philadelphia in 1776, Paine wanted to persuade ordinary colonists to support independence, so he used plain, forceful language, and his claim that freedom had been "hunted round the globe" was meant to move readers more than to describe every case accurately. Even so, the American Declaration of Independence soon echoed his challenge to hereditary authority. Mary Wollstonecraft extended the logic of reason to gender, demanding "a revolution in female manners" and women's power "over themselves" (Document 3). Because she was responding to Rousseau and wrote for educated readers, her argument focused on education rather than political rights, and she did not claim that women should rule men. Olympe de Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman (1791) shows that some contemporaries asked for more.

Ideas about labor and the economy also unsettled older hierarchies. Marx and Engels described history as "the history of class struggles" and called on workers to overthrow their rulers (Document 4). Writing for a political organization in 1848, they had reason to emphasize conflict and to treat workers as a unified force, which most British workers were not at the time. Samuel Smiles, in contrast, told readers that growth came from individual effort and that excessive government help made people "helpless" (Document 5). Writing for readers hoping to rise, Smiles challenged the idea that birth fixed a person's place, but he also argued against state help, a position that fit the interests of a growing middle class. Adam Smith's account of pin-making (Document 2) shows how the division of labor increased output, laying groundwork for factory production that would create both new wealth and the workers whom Marx described as an "appendage of the machine."

However, new ideas also reinforced hierarchies. Marx and Engels observed that capitalism "compels all nations" to adopt its mode of production (Document 6), but they also portrayed European industry as forcing other societies into a subordinate position. Mill, an official of the East India Company, argued that liberty applied only to people capable of improvement by free discussion and that despotism was legitimate for "barbarians" (Document 7). Because he worked for the company that governed much of India, his view helped justify colonial rule at a time when Britain was expanding its empire. The Indian Rebellion of 1857 and the partition of Africa after 1884 show how liberal states applied liberty selectively.

In conclusion, new ideas weakened hierarchies based on birth and absolute monarchy, but they also created class divisions and gave new justifications for empire, so they challenged existing hierarchies without ending inequality.

Treating Marx and Engels as speaking for all workers.
Quoting Mill without noting his employment by the East India Company.
Writing “the author is biased” without explaining how that affects the argument.

options.modelResponse:
Both the Ottoman and Mughal Empires grew out of Turkic and Mongol traditions of conquest and Islamic rule. After the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and Babur defeated the Delhi sultan at Panipat in 1526, each empire ruled large populations that did not share the ruler's faith, including Christians and Jews in the Ottoman lands and a Hindu majority in northern India.

The Ottoman and Mughal Empires were similar in practical accommodation of non-Muslims within states led by Sunni rulers, but they differed in method: the Ottomans organized religious communities into semi-self-governing groups, while the Mughals under Akbar tried to bring Hindu elites into the ruling class, though later policy shifted under Aurangzeb.

Both empires accepted that non-Muslims could practice their religions. Ottoman rulers allowed Christians and Jews to worship and to pay the jizya in exchange for protection, and in 1492 Sultan Bayezid II welcomed Jews expelled from Spain. Akbar likewise permitted Hindu worship, and in the early Mughal period non-Muslims also paid the jizya until he abolished it in 1564. In each case, rulers valued the stability and tax revenue that came from keeping diverse subjects content.

The empires differed in how they organized that diversity. The Ottomans formalized the millet system, in which Orthodox Christians, Armenians, and Jews ran their own courts and schools under religious leaders who answered to the sultan. By contrast, Akbar integrated Hindu leaders directly into the state. He married Rajput princesses, gave Rajputs high ranks in the mansabdar system, and promoted a policy of sulh-i-kul, or peace with all. Ottoman integration of non-Muslims was more through separate communities; Mughal integration was more through shared offices.

Policy also changed over time in the Mughal case. Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679 and ordered some temples destroyed, and his long wars with the Marathas, Rajputs, and Sikhs strained the empire. The Ottoman system was more stable over this period, though Ottoman rulers treated Shi'a as threats during the wars against the Safavids.

In conclusion, both empires governed religious diversity pragmatically, but the Ottomans relied on separate, self-governing communities while Akbar's Mughals integrated Hindu elites into the state, a policy later reversed with costly consequences.

Using dates outside 1500 to 1750 as the main evidence.

options.modelResponse:
By the 1770s, Enlightenment writers such as Locke and Rousseau had argued that governments rested on the consent of the governed, and European empires in the Americas depended on trade and plantation labor. Wars such as the Seven Years' War had left Britain and France with large debts, which led both governments to seek more revenue from their colonies.

The American and Haitian Revolutions were similar in that both drew on Enlightenment ideas and resentment of imperial control, but they differed because the Haitian Revolution began among enslaved people and ended slavery, while the American Revolution kept slavery in place.

Both revolutions were shaped by Enlightenment principles. American colonists objected to taxes such as the Stamp Act of 1765 that were imposed without their consent, and the Declaration of Independence in 1776 declared that people had natural rights. In Saint-Domingue, the French Revolution's Declaration of the Rights of Man in 1789 inspired free people of color, who demanded the same rights as white colonists, and then enslaved people, who revolted in 1791. In both cases, a colonial population challenged rulers who seemed to violate principles of liberty.

The causes also differed. The American Revolution was mainly led by colonial elites, including merchants and planters, who wanted political autonomy and an end to British economic regulation. The Haitian Revolution grew from the brutal conditions of the sugar plantations, where enslaved Africans outnumbered whites and free people of color by a wide margin, and it was led by formerly enslaved leaders such as Toussaint Louverture.

Their outcomes diverged as well. The new United States created a constitution in 1787 and a republic, but it preserved slavery and excluded women and Native Americans from political rights. Haiti's leaders abolished slavery, defeated Napoleon's army, and in 1804 created the first independent state in Latin America founded by formerly enslaved people. Yet Haiti paid a heavy price: France demanded an indemnity of 150 million francs in 1825 in exchange for recognition, and many nations refused to trade with the new state, which limited its economic growth.

In conclusion, both revolutions grew from Enlightenment ideas and anti-imperial resentment, but Haiti's revolution was more radical in who it freed and more costly in its aftermath.

modelNotes.label: Analysis and reasoning

options.modelResponse:
After the First World War, many economies relied on loans from the United States, and when the New York stock market crashed in 1929, those loans stopped and trade collapsed. Germany, which was already burdened by war debts and the memory of hyperinflation in 1923, suffered some of the worst unemployment in the world, and by 1932 about six million Germans were out of work. In the United States, unemployment reached about a quarter of the workforce by 1933.

The governments of the United States and Germany were similar in that both expanded state control of the economy to fight unemployment, but they differed because the New Deal aimed at relief and reform within a democracy while Nazi Germany directed the economy toward rearmament and rejected democratic limits.

Both governments used public works and government direction to put people to work. In the United States, Franklin Roosevelt's New Deal created the Civilian Conservation Corps and the Works Progress Administration, which employed millions in building roads, bridges, and parks. In Germany, the Nazi government that took power in 1933 funded public works, including the autobahn highways, and sharply increased spending on the military. Both showed that governments were willing to take a larger role in the economy than they had before the Depression.

The differences were also significant. The New Deal sought to relieve distress and prevent a repeat of the crash through reforms such as bank deposit insurance and the Social Security Act of 1935, while leaving private property and elections in place. Nazi economic policy was designed to prepare for war and to reduce dependence on imports. The government directed industry under the Four-Year Plan of 1936, suppressed labor unions, and persecuted Jews and other groups, who were forced out of jobs. German unemployment fell mainly because of rearmament and conscription, not because of reforms meant to make the economy fairer.

The results also differed. The United States recovered slowly and still had high unemployment in 1938, but it preserved democratic government. Germany reduced unemployment faster but did so through policies that led toward war.

In conclusion, both governments expanded their economic role, but the United States did so to relieve hardship within a democratic framework, while Nazi Germany did so to build a militarized, authoritarian state.

modelNotes.label: Analysis and reasoning

Claiming the New Deal ended the Depression by itself.
Treating Germany's falling unemployment as proof of a healthy economy.
Ignoring the political differences between a democracy and a dictatorship.
